\paragraph{Implications and boundary conditions.}
Exception events capture 23--27pp of the ${\sim}$25pp headroom over source code, while complete traces recover only 3--6pp---counter to the assumption that more information helps \citep{chen2025tracepile,wang2025dcsh}.
However, verdict prediction is a structurally constrained diagnostic setting; these findings may not transfer to fault localization or program repair, where trace content carries non-redundant information.
TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} shows that selective trace extraction \emph{improves} fault localization, suggesting trace utility varies with task complexity.
Training solutions were sampled from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct; whether the signal hierarchy generalizes to human-written code with different exception distributions is untested.

\section{Conclusion}

Complete execution traces degrade SFT verdict prediction by 18--23pp compared to compact exception events across four code-specialized models (1.5B--13B, three families).
Since exception events structurally encode verdict direction, the high ceiling (${\geq}$99.33\%) is a structurally expected pattern; the contribution is quantifying and decomposing the degradation mechanism.
Controlled gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of this gap to training-time dilution; the dominant factor is inference-time signal sparsity, where diagnostic tokens are too sparse (${\sim}$1/500) for reliable extraction from verbose traces.
For practitioners, exception extraction is the recommended default; when unavailable, tail-truncated traces (${\geq}$512 tokens) recover 93--98\%.
These findings are specific to verdict prediction (a structurally constrained binary task); trace utility may differ for fault localization or program repair where richer context carries non-redundant information \citep{huang2026tracecoder}.
Within the ${\leq}$13B code-specialized regime studied, input density outweighs model scale (7B SFT surpasses GPT-4o by 12pp under compact input); whether this holds at 30B+ or for general-purpose LLMs remains open.

\section{Conclusion}

Complete execution traces degrade SFT verdict prediction by 18--23pp compared to compact exception events across four models (1.5B--13B, three families).
The exception ceiling (${\geq}$99.33\%) is structurally expected; the contribution is decomposing the degradation: gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% to training-time dilution, assigning the remainder to inference-time signal sparsity (${\sim}$1/500 diagnostic token ratio).
For practitioners, exception extraction is the recommended default; tail-truncated traces (${\geq}$512 tokens) recover 93--98\% when exceptions are unavailable.
Within the ${\leq}$13B code-specialized regime studied, input density outweighs model scale; whether this holds at 30B+ or for general-purpose LLMs remains open (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Exception ceiling as structural expectation.}
The near-perfect accuracy of \texttt{exception\_only} is partially tautological: exception events directly encode verdict direction (exception present $\to$ fail, absent $\to$ pass).
A regex matching exception class names achieves 93.61\% (B4, Table~\ref{tab:ablation}); an oracle over \texttt{exception\_type\_only} reaches 100\% on the training set (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
We therefore do not claim the exception ceiling itself as a novel finding.
The non-trivial contribution is twofold: (1)~quantifying that complete traces---which \emph{contain} all exception information---degrade accuracy by 18--23pp, and (2)~decomposing this degradation into gradient dilution (${\leq}$4\%) and inference-time signal sparsity (${\geq}$96\%) via controlled ablation.

For practitioners, exception extraction is the recommended default; tail-truncated traces (${\geq}$512 tokens) recover 93--98\% when exceptions are unavailable.
Within the ${\leq}$13B code-specialized regime studied, input density outweighs model scale; whether this holds at 30B+ or for general-purpose LLMs remains open (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
